Weak-SGD signal attenuation is a plausible explanation, not an isolated causal finding. Backtesting a rectifier-over-smooth preference despite one fewer LayerNorm gave 3 hits/1 miss in history, but only 1 hit/1 miss across two comparable weak-SGD lab sets, with median loss ratio approximately 1.00. That evidence does not justify a general override or a rule predicting the complete gold order.

q16 comment: I overestimated normalization’s loss of radial information and underestimated its optimization benefit. C normalizes learned, biased ReLU features—not raw coordinates—so radius is not simply erased. Normalization can reduce outer-radius dominance and improve conditioning under small-step SGD; the controlled comparison supports this explanation, though it does not isolate those mechanisms. On another 1.5-turn spiral with the same width, budget, and optimizer, adding LN reduced mean CE from 0.64655 to 0.61061. Thus C deserved priority over B. No KB claim helped or misled me: I did not consult the KB. The other pairwise orderings were correct. For 1.5-turn two-spiral classification, a nonresidual width-64 ReLU MLP with one hidden block, trained for 2048 steps at batch size 16 using SGD with lr=0.0003, momentum=0.9, and weight decay=0.001, should achieve lower 10-seed mean test CE with LayerNorm before its hidden-block linear layer than without it.

Mechanism: normalization acts on a biased learned feature representation, retaining some radial information while controlling feature scale and improving finite-budget optimization. The prediction is directional; the independent controlled experiment measured a CE improvement of 0.03594.

Backtest: all 49 spiral questions in the older corpus yielded zero exact matched shallow LN/no-LN comparisons, so they provide no direct validation. Five exact matched nonresidual depth-1 comparisons in the lab favored LN in four cases and opposed it in one. Those broader comparisons used GELU or SiLU with Adam or RMSprop, so they are supporting context, not tests of the narrow SGD/ReLU rule. The new controlled experiment supplies one direct independent hit and zero misses. The broad-rule miss was a 1.5-turn GELU/Adam comparison at lr=0.0003, demonstrating that LN should not receive a universal preference across optimizer and activation regimes.
